title_ar: قال المحقق للسجين ... | شعر الشيخ محمد الحسن الددو كتبه في السجن قبل أن يطلق سراحه
title_en: The Interrogator Said to the Prisoner ... | A Poem by Sheikh Muhammad al-Hasan al-Dedew, Written in Prison before His Release
body_ar: قال المحقق للسجين. من أين نعلك ذا الثمين؟ و منَ اين ثوبك لا تكن كالمفســدين الخائنين الآخــذين مـن الخلي ج من اليسـار من اليمين يأتيهم التمويل من كل البلاد مــدى السنـيـن حتى من الأفغان أر ض البؤس، وكر البائسين فـهـنــاك للإرهـاب قــا عــدة تـعـيـن القاعدين جعلوا المسـاجــد كالبنو ك تعج بالمستثمرين قــل مـا تشاء ولا تحرِّ فْ عنــدنا الخبر اليقين جلباب زوجتك الذي تـدنـيـه خيـر الشاهدين من أين جاء ألم يكن مستغربا في القاطنين قال السجين مبادراً ومنَ اين لي ذا الأكسجين خـيــرات أرضــي أنـتـمُ أنهـبـتـمـوها الناهبين ومـنـعتـمـوها أهلها ال فـقـراء والـمـستضعـفـين وأردتــم أن تـمـنـعـوا خـيـرات رب العــالمين هلا ســألت ذوي الغلـو ل النـاهبين السالبين هلا سألت ذوي الفجو ر الفاسدين المفسدين هلا سألت ذوي البنو ك المترفين المســرفين هلا سألت الطامحيــ ن الطامعيـــن الخائفين هلا ســألـت الكـاسيـا ت العاريات وما يعـين أنا لست أسرق أو أغل من الخزينة والخزين أنا لست أنهب من مشا ريع الضعاف الجائعين أنا ما أخذت سوى الذي قد نلت من عرق الجبين أنا مـنـكـر لـلـظلم أك ــره مـوبـقـات الظالمين قال المحقـق: مه، فــإن لـنا رجــالاً آخــــرين مـن أهــل ديـنـك قـابـلـي ــن لكل ذا ومـؤيدين وبنـص مـذهب مـالـك والأشـعـري مؤصلين قال السجين: بمذهب ال ــعنقا ومالكٌ الحزين ما مـالــك والأشـعـري وصـحـبـهم بمنافقـين أتـريـد مـنــي أن أكـو ن كـهـؤلاء الضـائعين البائـعـيــن الدين بالــد نــيا لكل المشتريــن الـمـعــلـنـيـن ولاءهم لـلـظــالميـن المعتدين العـارفـيـن بـعـزف كـل العـازفـيـن الزافنين الجاهلـيـن المنكريــ ن لقـول خير المرسلين من يسبقون الظلم بالت تـســويغ عنه مدافعين جبناء عن تـبـيـيــن حق ق الله والحــق المبين جرءاء في سب الدعا ة المخلصين الصادقين رحمــاء بـالكـفـار والـ فـجـــار لا بـالـمسلمين ولكــل مـا قــال الـزعي ــم وما يـريد مروّجين ولكــل قـانــون يخــا لف شرعة الهادي الأمين وعلى المساجد والمعا هد والمحاضر هاجمين ساعين للتخـريــب للت تــعليـم فـيها مـانـعـيـن وتـراهــم في كــل حقــ ل للطغـاة مصفـقـيـن في الكافرين مسارعي ــن مع اليهود مطبعين ومن التعفـف والحجا ب والاحتشـــام منفرين وبشــاشة التلفاز مـن أهل التسنن ساخريـن ولقولهم تـنـفـك تســ مع في الإذاعة سامرين هل أنكروا نكــراً وهـل كـانوا بـعــرف آمرين أف لهم مــن ما جنيـ ـن فما أولاء بمـصلحين ما أصلحوا من أمر دنـ ـيا لا ولا من أمر دين فعليهـمُ غـضـب المهي ــمن إنهم حزب اللعين
body_en:
[Verse. Rendered as prose, line by line; the Arabic is the operative text.]

**The interrogator said to the prisoner:**

*Where did you get those costly shoes of yours? And where did your robe come from? Do not be like the corrupt, the treacherous, who take from the Gulf, from the left and from the right,*

*to whom the funding comes from every land, year upon year — even from the Afghans, land of misery, den of the wretched: for there is a base there for terrorism, which aids those who sit idle.*

*They have turned the mosques into banks, thronging with investors. Say what you like, but do not distort: we have the report for certain.*

*Your wife's jilbāb, which she lets down — best of witnesses — where did it come from? Was it not an odd thing among the local people?*

**The prisoner said, without pausing:**

*And where would I get this oxygen of mine from? The good things of my land — you are the ones who plundered them, you plunderers,*

*and withheld them from their own people, the poor and the oppressed; and you wanted to withhold the good things of the Lord of the Worlds.*

*Why did you not question those who embezzle, the plunderers, the despoilers? Why did you not question the debauched, the depraved, the corrupters?*

*Why did you not question the men of the banks, the luxurious, the prodigal? Why did you not question the grasping, the covetous, the fearful?*

*Why did you not question the women who are clothed yet naked, and all that goes with it?*

*I do not steal, nor do I pilfer from the treasury and its stores. I do not plunder the projects meant for the weak and the hungry.*

*I have taken nothing but what I came by from the sweat of my brow. I am one who rejects injustice; I loathe the ruinous deeds of the oppressors.*

**The interrogator said: Enough.**

*For we have other men, of your own religion, who accept all of this and endorse it, and who ground it in the very text (naṣṣ) of the school of Malik and of al-Ash'ari.*

**The prisoner said:**

*By the school of the phoenix and the heron! Malik and al-Ash'ari and their companions are no hypocrites.*

*Do you want me to become like those lost men, who sell religion for the world to every buyer,*

*who proclaim their loyalty to the oppressors, the transgressors; who know the playing of every player and every dancer;*

*ignorant, denying the word of the best of the messengers; who run ahead of injustice with excuses for it, defending it;*

*cowards when it comes to making plain the right of God and the manifest truth, yet bold in reviling the sincere and truthful callers to God;*

*merciful to the unbelievers and the dissolute, but not to the Muslims; promoters of everything the leader says and wants,*

*and of every law that runs counter to the way of the Guide, the Trustworthy; attacking the mosques, the institutes and the traditional schools (maḥāẓir),*

*striving for their ruin, barring teaching in them; you see them in every field applauding the tyrants,*

*hastening into the company of the unbelievers, normalising with the Jews; repelling people from chastity, from the veil and from modesty;*

*mocking the people of the Sunnah from the television screen; you never cease to hear their talk on the radio as they while away the night.*

*Did they ever denounce a wrong? Were they ever bidders of what is right? Fie on them — what libertines! These are no reformers.*

*They have set right no matter of this world, nor any matter of religion. Upon them, then, be the wrath of the Overseer (al-Muhaymin): they are the party of the accursed one.*

flags.arabic: فـهـنــاك للإرهـاب قــا عــدة تـعـيـن القاعدين ... مع اليهود مطبعين ... إنهم حزب اللعين
flags.context: the poem as a whole: an interrogation scene in which a named regime and its scholars are denounced
options: publish with a full contextual note (written in detention, a dialogue in which the first speaker is the interrogator, not the Sheikh)
publish the Arabic with the English withheld pending review
flags.note: EDITORIAL, highest priority in this slice. The poem contains: an accusation of terrorism financing put in the interrogator’s mouth with an unmistakable pun on al-Qaeda (قاعدة تعين القاعدين, "a base that aids those who sit"); a denunciation of scholars who "normalise with the Jews" (مع اليهود مطبعين — تطبيع is the specific term for normalisation with Israel); and a closing line calling named opponents "the party of the accursed one". Translated faithfully, neither softened nor strengthened. Two risks for an English readership: the opening stanzas are the INTERROGATOR speaking, and a reader landing mid-page can easily take them for the Sheikh’s own words; and the anti-normalisation and takfīr-adjacent language carries reputational and, in some jurisdictions, legal exposure. The publication decision belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh’s office (style guide section 12).

flags.context: the prisoner’s retort to the claim that regime scholars ground their position in the school of Malik and al-Ashʻari
options: "By the school of the phoenix and the heron!" — مالك الحزين is the Arabic name of the grey heron, so the line pairs two proverbial birds, the ʻanqāʼ and the heron, to say the school they invoke does not exist — while punning on the name Malik
"By the school of the ʻanqāʼ — and Malik is grieved!" — reading مالك as the jurist and الحزين as a predicate
"the school of the ʻanqāʼ and of a sorrowful Malik", a single sarcastic phrase
flags.note: The pun is the crux of the line and does not survive into English. مالك الحزين is a fixed zoological name (the grey heron) and the ʻanqāʼ is the proverbially non-existent phoenix, so the pairing brands the invoked madhhab a fiction; at the same time the surface reads as "and Malik is grieved". The very next line ("Malik and al-Ashʻari and their companions are no hypocrites") shows the attack is on those who invoke them, not on the imams. A reviewer must choose whether to footnote the pun or to pick one sense.

flags.arabic: وبشــاشة التلفاز مـن أهل التسنن ساخريـن
flags.context: describing the scholars the prisoner denounces
options: "mocking the people of the Sunnah from the television screen" (reading bi-shāshat, "by/on the screen of the television")
"mocking the people of the Sunnah with the affability of television" (reading bashāshah, "cheerfulness, affability")
"with the television’s smiling face, deriding the people of adherence to the Sunnah"
flags.note: The unvocalised بشاشة is exactly ambiguous between شاشة ("screen", with the preposition bi-) and بشاشة ("cheerfulness"). Both give good sense and both fit the metre. Not resolved.

flags.arabic: هلا ســألـت الكـاسيـا ت العاريات وما يعـين
flags.context: the end of the prisoner’s list of people the interrogator should have questioned instead
options: "and all that goes with it" (reading وما يُعِين as "and what abets it")
"and what that entails" (reading وما يَعْنِي, "and what it means")
the text is corrupt here and the phrase cannot be read with confidence
flags.note: The source is broken mid-word two words earlier (الكـاسيـا ت) and يعـين carries a tatweel, so the reading is not secure. The three options give materially different senses. Left unresolved rather than guessed.

flags.context: in the interrogator’s speech, of Afghanistan
options: "a base for terrorism there, which aids those who sit idle" — keeping the pun on al-Qaeda (القاعدة) and القاعدين flat in English
"there is al-Qaeda there, aiding those who sit back", naming the organisation outright
"there is a foundation for terrorism there that supports the idle"
flags.note: قاعدة/القاعدين is a deliberate double play: the organisation al-Qaeda, and the Qur’anic القاعدون, "those who sit back" from struggle. English can carry one or the other. Option 0 is preferred because the words are the interrogator’s insinuation, and naming the organisation outright would make the accusation more definite in English than it is in Arabic.

translator_notes: A poem in dialogue form, not a fatwa. type is set to "article" for want of a verse type in the schema. It contains no legal ruling and none has been inferred from it. The record should be displayed as poetry.

Rendered as prose, per style guide section 4. The speaker headings in bold are in the Arabic as قال المحقق / قال السجين and are not editorial additions; the line breaks are the translator’s, since the source runs the whole poem together as one block.

SOURCE DEFECT, severe. The Arabic as served is broken mid-word in roughly thirty places by stray spaces (الخلي ج for الخليج, أر ض for أرض, قــا عــدة for قاعدة, بالت تـســويغ for بالتسويغ, للت تــعليـم for للتعليم, حق ق for حق, مــن ما جنيـ ـن for من ماجنين) and is littered with tatweel elongation characters. This is the signature of text scraped out of a two-column layout. Every artefact is preserved verbatim in body_ar and none is reproduced in body_en. This should be cleaned corpus-wide, not per record (style guide section 11).

جلباب زوجتك الذي تدنيه echoes Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:59 (يدنين عليهن من جلابيبهن). The source does not mark it as a quotation, so it is translated as the speaker’s own words and the echo is noted here rather than turned into a citation.
رحماء بالكفار والفجار لا بالمسلمين inverts Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:29 (أشداء على الكفار رحماء بينهم). The inversion is the point of the line and has been kept literal.
الكاسيات العاريات is a phrase from a hadith in Sahih Muslim. The source gives no attribution and no grading, and none has been supplied (style guide section 4).
حزب اللعين in the closing line plays against حزب الشيطان / حزب الله of Sūrat al-Mujādilah 58:19-22; اللعين ("the accursed one") is a standard epithet for Satan. Rendered literally.

المحاضر in the penultimate movement is the plural of المحظرة, the Mauritanian traditional school, spelled here with ḍād as elsewhere in this range. Rendered "the traditional schools (maḥāẓir)" and the spelling left as found.
dec: A prison poem whose opening stanzas are the interrogator speaking — a reader landing mid-page takes them for the Sheikh’s own words — and whose closing lines are takfīr-adjacent.
